A.explanation: About 10 times too small. It results from an error converting $340 \text{ m}^3$ per minute to per second or in powers of ten to MW.

B.explanation: Mass flow is about $5.67 \times 10^3 \text{ kg s}^{-1}$, input $mgh$ rate is about $1.67 \text{ MW}$, and $90\%$ gives about $1.5 \text{ MW}$.

C.explanation: This is the input gravitational power $\rho Vgh/t$ of about $1.7 \text{ MW}$ before multiplying by the $0.90$ efficiency.

D.explanation: About 60 times too large. It uses $340 \text{ m}^3$ per minute as if it were per second, omitting division by $60$.

hints: Notice the flow is $340 \text{ m}^3$ per minute, but power is energy per second, so first convert the volume to $\text{m}^3 \text{ s}^{-1}$ and then to mass per second using density $1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$.
Connect the 30 m drop to loss of gravitational potential energy: input power equals mass per second times $gh$, with $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Calculate the $mgh$ power in watts, convert to MW, then multiply by $0.90$ because only 90% becomes useful output - compare with the 1.7 MW value before efficiency.
walkthrough: Identify the water supplied per second. $V/t = 340/60 \approx 5.67 \text{ m}^3 \text{ s}^{-1}$.
Convert to mass per second using $m = \rho V$. $m/t = 1000 \times 5.67 \approx 5667 \text{ kg s}^{-1}$.
State the input power as rate of loss of gravitational potential energy. $P_{in} = (m/t)gh$.
Apply efficiency for useful output. $P_{out} = 0.90 \times P_{in} \approx 0.90 \times 1.67 \approx 1.5 \text{ MW}$.
